structured_output.hypothesis: In measured cross-sectional US stature by single year of age, the yearly increment in height is largest in infancy, stays low and roughly constant across middle childhood, rises to a clear adolescent peak, and then falls to near zero by ages 18-19.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using survey-weighted median stature by sex (recumbent length under 2 years, standing height from 2 years) from pooled NHANES cycles, compute yearly increments (cm/yr) between consecutive integer ages 0-19. The claim passes if ALL of the following hold for BOTH sexes. (a) Infancy: the 0-1 yr increment is at least 2.0 times the mean increment over ages 6-9. (b) Steady childhood: increments between ages 4 and 10 each lie within 4.0-8.0 cm/yr, and max minus min over ages 6-10 is at most 2.0 cm/yr. (c) Teen quickening: the maximum increment in ages 10-15 exceeds the mean increment over ages 6-9 by at least 1.5 cm/yr. The peak must fall at ages 11-14 for boys and 10-13 for girls. (d) Arrest: the mean increment over ages 17-19 is below 1.0 cm/yr and below 25% of the adolescent peak increment. Bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples, respecting survey design) must not cross the thresholds in (a), (c) and (d).
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if for either sex any one of these holds. The adolescent peak increment is less than 1.5 cm/yr above the mean for ages 6-9. The 0-1 yr increment is less than 2.0 times the mean for ages 6-9. Childhood increments range by more than 2.0 cm/yr over ages 6-10. The mean increment over ages 17-19 is 1.0 cm/yr or more. The adolescent peak falls outside the stated windows.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'length or stature' is measured as recumbent length for infants and standing height for older children. 'Rate of growth' is the yearly increment in the median of the age-specific distribution. The data are cross-sectional, so these are synthetic velocity curves rather than longitudinal velocities. Because the pubertal spurt happens at different ages in different children, cross-sectional medians blur the spurt, and the test thresholds allow for this. 'Early boyhood' means ages about 4-10. 'The teens' and 'the growing age' mean the adolescent growth spurt. 'Gradual arrest' means velocity approaching zero near adult height. The test applies to both sexes, which is stricter than Thompson's wording about boys.

dataset.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), Body Measures (BMX) examination data
dataset.publisher: CDC National Center for Health Statistics
dataset.why_it_fits: NHANES records measured (not self-reported) stature for all ages. The BMX files give BMXRECUM (recumbent length, infants and toddlers) and BMXHT (standing height, age 2 and over). Demographics files give RIDAGEYR and RIDAGEMN (age in years and months), RIAGENDR (sex) and the survey weights (WTMEC2YR). Pooling cycles gives enough sample to compute weighted medians by single year of age and bootstrap CIs for the increments. Files are free to download as SAS XPT.
